page.h1: HTS Chapter 02: Meat and Edible Meat Offal — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Chapter 02 Export Rules: USDA FSIS Certificates & Schedule B
seo.shortDescription: What a U.S. meat exporter must do before shipping: Schedule B, USDA FSIS export certificate, plant eligibility, buyer screening and AES.

intro: Exporting meat from the U.S. is routine except for one thing: almost every shipment needs a USDA FSIS export certificate, issued only for product from a plant that the destination country has accepted. After that, the steps are the usual ones: find the Schedule B number, screen the buyer and file the export in AES. Meat is EAR99, so no Commerce licence applies in the ordinary case. Some buyers add programs of their own, such as China's ban on ractopamine in pork. Cuba is a real buyer of U.S. poultry but is sold under special rules.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Most trade is in a few lines: frozen pork cuts (0203.29), frozen chicken cuts and paws (0207.14), boneless beef (0201 and 0202), and variety meats (0206). The first six digits are the HS code on the Overview.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Meat is sold through many brokers and distributors. Screen every consignee and the ultimate buyer, including when product ships through a trading hub such as Hong Kong.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Fresh, chilled and frozen meat and offal are EAR99, so no Commerce licence is needed unless the destination or end user is restricted (see the sanctions step).

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: Cuba bought about $340 million of Chapter 02 goods in 2025. Food sales to Cuba are allowed only under the Trade Sanctions Reform Act, with payment in cash in advance or through a third-country bank and a notice to BIS before shipping (License Exception AGR). Check the current OFAC and BIS rules before quoting.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: A pallet of meat is almost always over $2,500 per Schedule B number, so file in AES.

rules.agency: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS)
rules.title: Export certificate: meat and poultry products for export need an FSIS export certificate, issued by an FSIS inspector (or through the PHIS e-certification system) after confirming the plant is eligible for the destination country. FSIS's Export Library lists each country's requirements and eligible plants.

rules.agency: USDA FSIS and USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS)
rules.title: China-specific programs: pork for China must come from hogs raised under AMS's Never Fed Beta Agonists program or a written ractopamine-free program, and negative test results alone are not enough. FSIS's China page also lists beef conditions and a plant attestation. Check the live Export Library before each shipment.

citations.label: AMS: Never Fed Beta Agonists program

rules.title: Rabbit and game: rabbit meat and some other meat in 0208 are not under FSIS's mandatory inspection, so the export certificate is issued through USDA's voluntary inspection programs when the buyer asks for one.

Cuba: food sales are allowed only under the Trade Sanctions Reform Act. OFAC's regulation sets the payment terms (cash in advance or financing by a third-country bank), and BIS's License Exception AGR requires a notification before shipping agricultural commodities.

groups.label: Meat of bovine animals, fresh or chilled
groups.note: Beef: FSIS export certificate from a plant on the buyer's list. Korea limits beef to cattle under 30 months old.

groups.label: Meat of bovine animals, frozen
groups.note: Same as fresh beef. Frozen boneless beef is the largest line for Korea, Japan and China.

groups.label: Meat of swine, fresh, chilled, or frozen
groups.note: Pork for China needs an AMS Never Fed Beta Agonists or ractopamine-free program on top of the certificate.

groups.label: Meat of sheep or goats, fresh, chilled or frozen
groups.note: Lamb and mutton: routine FSIS certificate and plant eligibility.

groups.label: Meat of horses, asses, mules or hinnies, fresh, chilled or…
groups.note: Almost no U.S. exports: federal inspection of horse slaughter for food is not funded, so commercial horse meat for export is very rare.

groups.label: Edible offal of bovine animals, swine, sheep, goats…
groups.note: Variety meats are the largest line for China; the same FSIS certificate and plant eligibility apply, and pork offal for China follows the pork program.

groups.label: Meat and edible offal, of the poultry of heading 0105…
groups.note: Poultry (chicken cuts, paws, turkey): FSIS certificate under 9 CFR Part 381. Cuba is a top poultry buyer and has its own sanctions rule.

groups.label: Other meat and edible meat offal, fresh, chilled or frozen
groups.note: Rabbit and game: a certificate through voluntary inspection if the buyer asks.

groups.label: Pig fat, free of lean meat, and poultry fat, not rendered…
groups.note: Pig and poultry fat: routine FSIS certificate.

groups.label: Meat and edible meat offal, salted, in brine, dried or…
groups.note: Ham, bacon and other cured meat: routine FSIS certificate and plant eligibility.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
